entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The World Bank Group, established in 1944 during the Bretton Woods Conference in the United States, is a consortium of five international institutions dedicated to providing financial and technical assistance to developing countries. Headquartered in Washington, D.C., its primary mission is to reduce poverty and promote sustainable economic development through loans, grants, and expertise. Notable figures involved in its inception include John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White, who played pivotal roles in shaping the post-World War II economic landscape. As a key player in global finance, the World Bank Group has significantly influenced international development policies and practices across continents.

Initially formed to facilitate reconstruction in war-torn Europe, the World Bank Group evolved into a broader institution focused on alleviating poverty in developing nations. By the 1960s, it expanded its scope to include projects in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, emphasizing infrastructure development, education, and health. The International Development Association (IDA), established in 1960, provided concessional loans to the poorest countries, while the International Finance Corporation (IFC), founded in 1956, aimed to promote private sector investment. Over the decades, the Group has approved over $1 trillion in loans and grants, impacting millions of lives through projects aimed at improving access to clean water, education, and economic opportunities.
